key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn spurious tool-use shortcuts, calling tools from superficial cues instead of real task need, but a tool-necessity reward can suppress this behavior.
engineering_relevance: For agentic systems, tool routing should be trained and audited as a safety-critical policy because competence with a tool can itself trigger cue-driven misuse.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue-to-tool correlations during training.
Tested counterfactual cases where cues remained but tools were unnecessary, measuring shortcut tool invocation.
Added a dense decision-level reward from an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was actually needed.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared mainly after the agent had already learned the tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward can reduce shortcut use, but its effectiveness depends on the judge’s accuracy and consistency in judging tool necessity.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
